D018-D019_h001.question:
I’ve been having a hard time since that nighttime fare last February—guy got violent, pulled a knife, made me drive at gunpoint. Even though it’s been over four months now, I keep seeing it like it’s happening all over again. Outta nowhere, I’ll be stuck in traffic or clocking in for a shift, and boom—I’m back in that car, heart pounding, hands shaking.  

The worst part is the noise. Every honk, every slamming door? I jolt like I’ve been shocked. Sometimes I even flinch so hard I drop my keys. My thoughts feel foggy, like I’m walking through thick air. I can’t focus, can’t remember streets I’ve driven for years.  

I don’t care about work like I used to. Used to hustle extra shifts, save a bit—now, what’s the point? I just need to get through the day. And that guy who put me in that situation… it wasn’t just him. The dispatcher knew he was late at night, wouldn’t check in. Feels like they all left me hanging.  

I’m always on edge, like something’s about to go wrong. It’s not just anxiety—it’s constant, like my body won’t calm down. And it’s been like this since March. Not just a few weeks. Longer. Every day feels like I’m still in that car.
D018-D019_h001.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D018-D019_h002.question:
I’ve been feeling completely numb since it happened—like, nothing brings me joy anymore. I used to love hanging out with friends, even just small things like listening to music or tasting the new syrups we’d get at the café, but now it’s all just… empty. I don’t even cry. I can’t feel love, not even for my mom. And I’m constantly angry—just this simmering rage, like the world owes me something. I catch myself snapping at customers over nothing. It’s not fair—it was *their* fault, not mine. Those people just came out of nowhere and—

Sometimes, even seeing someone move too fast behind the counter makes me jump. My chest tightens. Once, a regular customer walked in fast through the front door, and I actually flinched so hard I dropped a cup. It’s been happening for weeks. Thinking’s been hard too—like my head’s stuck in fog. I can’t focus on the orders, forget names, mix up drinks. I didn’t think it’d still be like this after a month. I hoped it would just go away, but if anything, it’s getting worse.
D018-D019_h002.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D018-D019_h003.question:
I’m 70, been on my own since my husband passed five years back. I used to love gardening—had the most beautiful roses on the block—but these days, I can’t even stand being outside when the wind picks up. That storm last April… the tornado warning, the basement, the way the house groaned like it was alive… I still feel it in my bones. When someone touches my shoulder unexpectedly, I flinch so hard I’ve knocked things over. My heart pounds, my hands go cold—it’s like I’m back in that basement, frozen, feeling the walls shake.

I don’t enjoy much anymore. Used to knit for the grandchildren, but now it feels pointless. I keep thinking, *If the neighbors had warned us sooner, if they’d taken the threat seriously*, instead of waiting—why didn’t they say something? That moment—the deafening roar, the sheer terror—plays in my head like a broken record. I can’t clear the fog in my thoughts; I forget what I came into a room for, or lose track of time.

It’s been over six months now. I thought I’d regain myself, but it’s only gotten worse. The fear doesn’t fade—it’s still right here.
D018-D019_h003.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D018-D019_h004.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since that incident during the executive protection detail six months ago—when the explosion went off near the car. I can still hear it. Sometimes, out of nowhere, I’m back there—I feel the heat, the panic, my body tenses like I’m frozen in the moment. It’s like I’m reliving it, even when I know I’m not. It happens when a car backfires or something drops loudly. I jump hard, sometimes knock things over. My hands shake.  

I used to take pride in being sharp, decisive—one step ahead. Now I stand in the grocery aisle second-guessing what to eat, what shirt to buy. Feels pointless, honestly. What’s the point of success when everything could blow up without warning? I don’t care much about advancing or even staying in this job.  

And I can’t stop thinking it could’ve been avoided. If the intel team had flagged that van, or if command hadn’t cut corners, maybe none of it would’ve happened. I know that might not be fair, but that’s how it sits.  

I’m always on edge. Can’t relax. Haven’t been able to sleep without the nightmares for more than a month now—ever since it happened.
D018-D019_h004.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D018-D019_h005.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since that accident last year—hit a guardrail during a storm, rolled the truck, nearly didn’t make it out. Ever since, I can’t even hear a siren or see flashing lights and not get this knot in my chest. My hands shake, heart races, and it takes me ages to calm down. Even driving on wet roads now makes me feel like I’m back there.

It’s been over a year, and I’m still not right. I used to take pride in my work, hitting those long routes, staying clean on my record—but now, I just don’t care. Doesn’t matter if I get a bonus or a clean log. My wife says I’ve changed. I get angry easy—little things set me off. I find myself blaming the dispatcher, like she pushed me out in that storm on purpose. It’s not fair, I know, but I can’t shake it.

Making choices feels impossible. What to eat, what shirt to wear—even small stuff has me stuck for minutes. I jump at loud noises and then just… vibrate for ages afterward. I used to bounce back. Not anymore. It’s like the whole thing got locked inside me and won’t let go.
D018-D019_h005.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Acute Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D018-D019_h006.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since that warehouse fire last year—seven months ago now. I was inside during the initial explosion, and two of my crew didn’t make it out. Ever since, I can’t stand going near flames, even a lighter. If someone lights a cigarette around me, I freeze up, my chest tightens. I avoid the route we used to take to the site—I had to ask for a transfer just so I wouldn’t pass by.  

I don’t remember much from the fire itself—whole chunks are just gone. Sometimes I think that’s a blessing, but it eats at me too. I can’t explain it. My wife took me to a concert last month—something we haven’t done in years—and I smiled when she was happy, but I didn’t *feel* it. Nothing gives me that lift anymore.  

I’m always on edge. My daughter startled me when she came around the corner at home last week—just walked in quietly—and I nearly tackled her. I yelled before I even saw her. I’m tired of being like this. It’s not just the memories. It’s been too long. I thought I’d get past it, but it’s only gotten worse.
D018-D019_h006.options:
A. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h007.question:
I’ve been kind of unraveling since that warehouse fire last year—man, I still see the flames when I close my eyes. I work with electrical systems now, and sometimes a spark or the smell of burnt wire hits me and I can’t breathe—my chest tightens, hands shake, like I’m right back there. I don’t go near job sites with heavy smoke or alarms anymore. I just tell my crew I’m not feeling it, but really, I can’t risk it.  

It’s like… big chunks of that night are just gone. I remember arriving, the heat, then waking up in the hospital—but not how I got out. The guys say I pulled two people out before the collapse, but I don’t remember any of it.  

I used to call my mom every week, but now I can’t even look at her texts. It’s not that I don’t care—I just feel hollow. My girlfriend left last month. Said I never talk, never touch her. I wanted to love her, but it was like the switch got flipped off.  

Little things set me off—door slams, horns—I jump, sometimes drop what I’m holding. And if someone questions me on the job, I snap—yell, curse, don’t care. It’s been like this for nearly nine months. I thought it’d fade by now, but it’s only getting heavier.
D018-D019_h007.options:
A. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h008.question:
I’ve been having these intense flashbacks—like I’m back there in the car again, smelling the smoke, hearing the crunch of metal. It hits out of nowhere during class or while I’m trying to sleep. I don’t talk about the accident, not even with my parents. Honestly, I can’t remember parts of it—like how I got out of the car—but I remember the blood on the steering wheel. It’s messed up.  

I used to love basketball, hanging out with my friends after school, but nothing feels good anymore. My mom took me to a movie last week, and I just sat there, empty. And I’m always on edge. Someone drops a book in the hall, and I’m jumping, heart slamming, hands shaking. It takes forever to calm down. My teacher asked me a simple question yesterday, and I snapped at him—like, really yelled. I didn’t mean to.  

This started right after the crash last February—so it’s been more than a month now. At first, I thought it’d fade, but it’s not. It’s like the accident keeps happening, over and over, and I can’t get past it.
D018-D019_h008.options:
A. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h009.question:
I’m a line cook at a busy downtown restaurant—well, I *was*—but I haven’t stepped foot in the kitchen in over three months. It started after a fire broke out in the prep area. I got out okay, but one of my guys didn’t make it. Ever since, I can’t stand the sound of the vent hood kicking on or a pan clanging—anything loud—and when it happens, I jump like I’ve been shocked, sometimes dropping whatever I’m holding. I keep replaying bits of that night, but it’s weird—some parts are crystal clear, like the color of the flames, but I can’t remember how I got out or what I said right after. It’s like my brain just blanks on the middle.  

I’ve stopped going downtown. Won’t drive past the restaurant, won’t even talk about work. My wife says I’ve gone quiet—like I’m there but not feeling anything, not joy, not sadness, just… nothing. Little things set me off though. Last week I screamed at a neighbor for knocking too hard on the door. I feel like I’m wired wrong now. This isn’t getting better. It’s been four months, and honestly, it feels worse than ever.
D018-D019_h009.options:
A. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h010.question: I’ve been struggling ever since that assault happened—nine months ago. I still remember bits, but it’s like my mind shut down during it; I can’t recall most of what happened, which terrifies me. Whenever I hear a loud noise, like a door slamming at the office, I flinch hard—sometimes drop my pen or spill my coffee. My heart races, my hands get clammy. It’s humiliating. I try not to think about it, but certain smells or voices bring it all rushing back, so I avoid talking about it, even with my therapist. I don’t even go out with coworkers after work, even when they invite me. Honestly, nothing feels good anymore. I used to love designing, getting lost in color and layout, but now it’s just… nothing. I don’t feel joy, not even when I get positive feedback. Last week, a colleague startled me by tapping my shoulder, and I threw my tablet down—cracked the screen. I didn’t mean to, but I just exploded. I’ve been like this for so long now—way more than a month. I thought I’d get over it, but it’s only gotten harder to function.
D018-D019_h010.options:
A. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h011.question:
I’ve been a forest ranger for over forty years—used to find peace in the woods, but not anymore. Ever since that wildfire two years ago, when I couldn’t save one of the hikers caught in the flames, things haven’t been right. I keep seeing his face when I close my eyes, and even the smell of smoke from a campfire makes me shake and feel like I can’t breathe. I try not to talk about it or think about it, but the memories just come, uninvited. I’ve stopped going to community meetings or even visiting my son—just easier to stay out in the backcountry alone.

I don’t trust anyone much these days. I keep thinking people won’t understand, or worse, they’ll blame me too—like I didn’t do enough. Sometimes I get angry for no reason—just snap at folks over little things, even good people just checking in. My wife passed a few years back, and now I feel like the world just keeps taking. It’s not just that one bad week after the fire—I’ve felt this way for months and months. Over a year now, honestly. I thought I’d bounce back, but it’s only gotten deeper.
D018-D019_h011.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h012.question:
I’m 67 and have been volunteering at the community center since I retired—used to bring me so much joy. But since the car accident last year, where I lost my dear friend who was in the passenger seat, things haven’t been right. It’s been over four months now, and I still can’t drive past that intersection—my chest tightens, my hands shake, I feel like I’m back in that moment. I’ve stopped going to the grocery store because one of the volunteers drives a car that looks just like the one that hit us. 

I avoid talking about it with anyone, even my daughter. Honestly, I don’t talk about much at all anymore. A part of me believes I should’ve swerved sooner—that I failed her. I feel broken, like I don’t deserve to move on. Sometimes I get so angry—at the driver, at myself, even at my friend for suggesting we take that route. I snapped at a fellow volunteer last week over a misplaced clipboard. I’ve never been that way before. These feelings… they’re not letting up. If anything, they’re heavier than they were months ago.
D018-D019_h012.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h013.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since that car accident three months ago—my husband was seriously hurt, and I still see it when I close my eyes. Every time I hear a loud noise or a screech on the road, my heart races and I start shaking, like I’m right back there. I try not to think about it, but certain things—a red minivan, the smell of gasoline—pull me right into it. I avoid talking about it, even with my husband, because just saying the words makes me feel like I’m suffocating.

Since then, it’s been hard to trust anyone. I used to be friendly with parents at school, but now I keep thinking, “What if they’re hiding something? What if they’re dangerous?” I’ve even snapped at a few of them—yelling during pickup because I thought they were being careless with their kids. It’s not like me. I blame the driver who hit us, but sometimes I get angry at the paramedic too—like he didn’t help fast enough. I just can’t shake the feeling that the world isn’t safe anymore. This isn’t getting better—it’s been over a month, and I feel worse.
D018-D019_h013.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h014.question: I work as a sommelier, which means I’m often in fast-paced, crowded restaurants where things get loud and unpredictable. About three months ago, I was walking home after a dinner service when I was mugged at knifepoint. Ever since, I can’t seem to reset. I keep having these intense dreams—reliving the moment he came at me, the fear, the helplessness—sometimes I wake up drenched in sweat. I try not to think about it during the day, but memories just crash in, especially if I pass that alley. So I avoid that whole route, even if it’s longer. I’ve started believing the world’s just full of predators—can’t trust anyone, not really. I find myself blaming the guy who owned the corner store nearby; he didn’t intervene, didn’t even call the cops. Like he let it happen. On top of that, I snap easily—my manager asked me to open a bottle differently last week, and I nearly shouted at him. I’m on edge constantly, like danger’s always just around the corner. It’s been like this for over a month now—long past when I thought I’d feel normal again.
D018-D019_h014.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h015.question:
I’ve been having a real hard time since that accident six months ago—when my car got T-boned by a truck running a red light. I wasn’t seriously hurt, but I can’t get it out of my head. Whenever I hear a sudden horn or a screech of tires, my heart starts racing, my palms sweat, and I feel like I’m back in that moment. I’ve stopped driving completely—won’t even take the same route to work—and I avoid ride-shares if the driver speeds or cuts corners. Even sitting in traffic makes me feel trapped and panicked.

I used to trust people, but now I feel like everyone’s reckless or out to get you—like the world’s just full of danger. I catch myself blaming the other driver constantly, replaying it in my head, thinking if he hadn’t been so careless, my life wouldn’t be like this. I’ve snapped at coworkers over small things, once threw my coffee mug across the room during a flashback at my desk. I’m usually calm, but now I feel like I’m always on edge, waiting for the next disaster. It’s been months, and it hasn’t gotten better—only worse.
D018-D019_h015.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h016.question:
I’ve been off ever since that night at the library six months ago—when the man broke in during closing, screaming, waving a knife. I didn’t think I’d make it out. Even now, the sound of a chair scraping or someone walking too fast through the stacks makes my chest tighten and my hands shake. I don’t know how to explain it—I just *react*, like my body remembers before my mind does.  

I try not to talk about it, not even with my sister. Thinking about what happened just pulls me back there, so I push it away. But no matter how hard I try, I keep replaying it, especially at night. I’ve started snapping at coworkers who don’t understand why I won’t take evening shifts anymore. It’s not their fault, but I can’t help feeling like the guards, even the police that night—they were too slow. They should’ve been there sooner.  

And I’m just… always on edge. At home, I check the locks three times. I can’t sit with my back to the door. Even in my own apartment, I don’t feel safe. It’s exhausting. This has been going on since the incident—longer than I ever thought it would. Six months, and I still feel like I’m running from something I can’t escape.
D018-D019_h016.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h017.question:
I’ve been feeling completely on edge since it happened—almost two months ago now. I was held up at knifepoint walking home from work one night, and since then, I can’t stop seeing it play out in my head. Out of nowhere, I’ll get these flashes—the glint of the blade, his voice—like I’m right back there. It’s constant and I can’t shut it off.

I used to take the same route to the mall every evening, but now I won’t even go near that block. I’ve started avoiding certain customers too, especially if someone stands too close or speaks too fast. It just sets something off in me. My manager’s noticed I’ve been passing shifts to others—I can’t explain why, but being around strangers feels risky.

And honestly? I keep thinking about how the security guard at the subway ignored me when I looked scared earlier that night. If he’d said something, maybe it wouldn’t have happened. I know that sounds harsh, but I can’t shake this feeling that someone else should’ve stepped in.

I’m always watching now—checking doorways, sizing people up, listening too closely. It's exhausting. I didn’t used to be like this—I used to feel safe in the city. Now, it’s like the world’s full of threats I used to ignore.
D018-D019_h017.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h018.question:
I’ve been struggling ever since that call back in April—nine months ago now. We got dispatched to a vacant house with a severe infestation, and I found someone… hanging. I can’t get the image out of my head. It just hits me outta nowhere, even when I’m trying to relax. I’ll see it so clear, like I’m back there. I don’t talk about it—haven’t even told my ex-wife the details. The truth is, I keep thinking I should’ve noticed something, should’ve checked the place differently when I came in. Maybe I could’ve helped. I know it wasn’t my job to save him, but it doesn’t feel that way inside.

Ever since, I can’t stop watching my surroundings—walking into a room, I immediately note the exits, check shadows, listen for odd sounds. It’s exhausting. At first, I thought it’d fade in a couple weeks, but here I am, half a year later, still on edge, jumping at noises, avoiding any job near that part of town. I used to handle the rough stuff fine, but now it’s like my mind’s stuck in that moment, and I can’t reset.
D018-D019_h018.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h019.question:
I’m a waste management officer—been at it for over twenty years. We don’t see the worst of things every day, but sometimes… sometimes it sticks. About eight months ago, we got a call to clear a dumpsite where they found human remains—burned, tangled in trash. I saw a lot growing up in this job, but this… this got inside my head. Ever since, I can’t shut it out. I keep reliving those images—outta nowhere, just there, like I’m back in that heat, smelling it all again. I try not to think about it, but the harder I push it down, the more it claws its way up at night. I blame myself, too—like I should’ve noticed something earlier, flagged it, done *something*. 

I’ve stopped going to similar sites if I can help it. Even in restaurants now, I don’t sit with my back to the door. I scan exits, check faces—gotta know where to go, just in case. My wife says I’m distant, jumpy. I haven’t been able to sleep through the night since that day. Honestly, I thought it’d fade after a few weeks, but it’s only gotten worse. It’s been months now, and I still feel like I’m stuck back there.
D018-D019_h019.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h020.question:
I’m a 23-year-old apprentice electrician, and about two months ago, I was on a job site when part of the ceiling collapsed. A beam hit my coworker—he didn’t make it. I wasn’t physically hurt, but since then, things haven’t been right. Out of nowhere, I’ll be wiring a junction box and suddenly feel like I’m back there—the dust in my eyes, the noise, him shouting. It’s like I’m reliving it, can’t move or think straight for a few seconds. I’ve started avoiding job sites with high ceilings, even turned down work. If I see a truck from that site, my chest locks up.  

I keep thinking it shouldn’t have happened—our supervisor ignored safety checks that morning. It’s not on us; it’s on him. I catch myself scanning rooms the second I walk in—exits, who’s near me, anything that feels off. I check the locks at home three times before bed. This isn’t just stress—it’s been over a month now, and it’s not fading. Some days feel worse than the first week. I can’t keep working like this.
D018-D019_h020.options:
A. Adjustment Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D019_h021.question:
I still see it all, every single day—the screech of tires, the shattered glass, the way my body just… flew. It happened four months ago now, when the truck ran the red light and hit me head-on. I survived, but since then, these flashes just come out of nowhere. I’ll be editing a campaign at work, and suddenly I’m back in the car, heart slamming, tasting blood. I can’t shut it off.

The fear hasn’t faded either. It’s like the moment of impact is frozen inside me. I used to be so warm with people—kissing my mom on the cheek, hugging my boyfriend—but now I can’t even cry. I look at him and feel nothing. It kills him, but I’m just… empty.

And the anger—I didn’t used to be like this. Last week, I threw my laptop across the room during a Zoom call because someone mislabeled a slide. I’ve snapped at coworkers, even shoved a colleague when they startled me from behind.

I know it’s been longer than a month, and nothing’s gotten better. If anything, it’s worse. I thought I’d bounce back, but I’m not.
